Adam Harris Skip to content Adam Harris I am an Assistant Professor of Economics at Cornell. I apply industrial organization tools to questions at the intersection of technology and transportation. My current research studies artificial intelligence and the US trucking industry. Office hours: By appointment using Calendly . CV (Updated June 2025) Published papers Long-Term Relationships in the US Truckload Freight Industry (with Thi Mai Anh Nguyen) AEJ: Microeconomics , Feb 2025 This paper provides evidence on relational contracting in the US truckload freight industry. In this setting, shippers and carriers engage in repeated interactions under contracts that fix prices but leave scope for inefficient opportunism. We describe empirically the strategies of shippers and the responses of carriers. We show that shippers use the threat of relationship termination to deter carriers from short-term opportunism. Carriers respond to the resultant dynamic incentives, behaving more cooperatively when their potential future rents are higher. While shippers and carriers often interact on multiple lanes, we show that separate relational contracts appear to govern transactions on each lane. Working papers Human Decision-Making with Machine Prediction: Evidence from Predictive Maintenance in Trucking (with Maggie Yellen) Best Paper by a Junior Researcher—International Transportation Economics Association 2025 Annual Conference In this paper, we study the role of predictive artificial intelligence (AI) in human decision-making. Using a rich decision-level data set from the maintenance of heavy-duty trucks, we document how the repair decision-making of expert technicians changes with the introduction of an AI tool designed to predict the risk of truck breakdowns. We develop and estimate a dynamic discrete choice model of technician decision-making. The resulting estimates show that technicians with the AI tool exhibit a substantially better ability to predict breakdown risk than those without the tool. This improvement in predictive ability translates into better outcomes: The AI tool reduces the total costs that technicians incur by $240-$480 per truck per year. This brings the technician close to the efficient frontier; only 15% more cost savings could be achieved by further improvements in the quality of decision-making. Kate Bundorf Professor Ashish Arora kate.bundorf@duke.edu ashish.arora@duke.edu (919) 613-9368 (919) 660-7746 Job Market Monopsony in the High-Skilled Migrant Labor Market: Evidence from H-1B Paper Petition Data (with Seohee Kim) Abstract: This paper assesses the extent of monopsony power in the labor market for highly skilled immigrants, focusing on employment concentration and its impact on wages. We obtained the universe of petitions to the H-1B visa program, the largest high- skilled immigration program in the U.S., through a FOIA request. We first discover that the H-1B labor market is 30% more concentrated than the broader U.S. labor market, with a steadily increasing trend over the past decade. We then examine the causal impact of high employment concentration on H-1B workers’ wages by leveraging the lottery system for over-the-cap H-1B applications. The random lottery win rates in each labor market alter employment concentration, as different-sized firms vary in demand for first-time H- 1B applicants, the only group subject to the lottery. Our results indicate that transitioning from the 25th to the 75th percentile of employment concentration results in a 12.2% wage decline, equivalent to a median salary loss of $10.5k. The wage effects of concentration are primarily borne by first-time H-1B applicants, whose visa status is tied to a single employer. As a suggestive mechanism to these wage effects, we also find evidence that higher concentration leads to less job mobility between H-1B employers. These findings collectively suggest that H-1B policy reform should consider lifting the employer tie for first-time applicants. My research in quantitative marketing focuses on loyalty programs, pricing, and platform markets. I am on the 2026–27 academic job market. Research Job Market Paper Transitioning to a Status-Based Loyalty Program: Evidence from a Quasi-Experimental Study with Arun Gopalakrishnan and Upender Subramanian Abstract Retailers increasingly move from a non-tiered loyalty program (LP), which offers the same benefits to all members, to a tiered LP, which offers differential benefits by status. Yet little is known about how such a transition affects existing customers, who are sorted into tiers based on their past behavior. Working with an online food and beverage retailer in South Asia, we designed a quasi-experiment in which a three-tier LP (Bronze, Silver, and Gold) was launched in one pilot market while other markets kept the old LP, and we combine matching with difference-in-differences and regression discontinuity designs. Orders fell in every tier, but contribution did not fall by much in any. Gold customers placed fewer but larger orders, raising contribution by 4.9%, while Bronze customers ordered 7.5% less with little change in contribution, as they now paid delivery fees. Silver did little for the tier as a whole. Customers who just qualified for Gold outperformed those who narrowly missed it, with no sign that they stretched their orders to unlock perks, pointing to the psychological effect of status. Gold customers with the largest balances, however, responded negatively, revealing a tradeoff between removing costly universal benefits and alienating the most engaged customers. Presented at the ISMS Marketing Science Conference (2025, 2026), Marketing Dynamics Conference (2026), Yale China India Insights Conference (2026), and University of Houston Marketing Doctoral Symposium (2025).
